learningObjectives: Explain the developmental sequence underlying embryonic neural development.
Identify the principal cells, structures and signals involved in embryonic neural development.
Connect embryonic neural development to later cognition and behaviour.
Interpret clinical findings without treating development as deterministic.

anatomy.label: Neural plate
anatomy.short: Specialised ectoderm committed toward nervous tissue
anatomy.detail: Neural induction converts a region of surface ectoderm into a thickened neural plate.
anatomy.clinical: Failure at this earliest stage can affect broad portions of the nervous system.

anatomy.label: Organising signals
anatomy.detail: Signals from the notochord, floor plate and surrounding tissues pattern the developing neural tissue.
anatomy.clinical: The same morphogen can produce different cell fates at different concentrations and times.

anatomy.label: Neural progenitors
anatomy.short: Self-renewing cells that generate neural lineages
anatomy.detail: Progenitors proliferate, then produce neurons and glia in tightly regulated sequences.
anatomy.clinical: Altered proliferation can change cortical size, lamination and later network capacity.

anatomy.label: Regionalisation
anatomy.short: Early tissue acquires future brain-region identity
anatomy.detail: The anterior neural tube is subdivided into forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain territories.
anatomy.clinical: Regional identity is established long before mature anatomy is recognisable.

interaction.title: Embryonic Neural Development sequence
interaction.instruction: Select a component, then run the sequence to follow development over time.

stages.label: Induce
stages.text: Surface ectoderm is instructed to adopt neural fate.

stages.label: Pattern
stages.text: Morphogen gradients establish axes and positional identity.

stages.label: Expand
stages.text: Progenitor cells proliferate within germinal zones.

stages.label: Differentiate
stages.text: Cells begin neuron- and glia-specific developmental programs.

quizBank.question: Neural induction most directly refers to:
quizBank.explanation: Neural induction is the early commitment of ectodermal cells toward nervous-system tissue.

quizBank.question: Morphogen gradients are important because they:
options: Assign positional identity in developing tissue
quizBank.explanation: Concentration and timing of morphogens help specify which cell types and regions develop.

quizBank.question: Neural progenitors primarily:
quizBank.explanation: Progenitors divide and later generate neurons and glia.

quizBank.question: Why can early developmental insults have broad effects?
options: They occur before many regions and lineages have separated
The brain is already fully mature
quizBank.explanation: Early processes contribute to many later structures, so disruption may propagate widely.

quizBank.question: Which statement best reflects modern developmental neuroscience?
options: Genes, signals, activity and environment interact
A fixed blueprint unfolds without feedback
All regions mature at the same rate
quizBank.explanation: Development is an interactive, staged process rather than a rigid linear script.
